source.title: Debate Training Reduces Reward Hacking in RLAIF
source.authors: Zachary Kenton; Lili Janzer; Rory Greig; Tian Huey Teh; Kirill Tyshchuk; Jonah Brown-Cohen; Harri Edwards; Senthooran Rajamanoharan; N. Siegel; Natasha Jaques; Rohin Shah

record.tranche_reason: The study trains a stronger policy using feedback from a weaker LLM judge and measures task accuracy and reward hacking, but uses RL from AI feedback and debate rather than fine-tuning on weak-model labels.
record.gate_note: The paper does not test ordinary weak-label fine-tuning. It does test whether a stronger policy trained with a weaker judge surpasses that judge, how judge strength affects training, and whether the policy exploits judge errors. The 45% performance-gap-recovered figure uses the RLAIF-A baseline and RLVR roofline, not the original weak-supervisor PGR denominator.
record.test_reason: A Gemini 2.5 Flash-class policy is RL-trained only on rewards from a frozen, weaker Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite judge. The study reports that the policy's accuracy exceeds the judge's own generative accuracy. It compares a training change (debate) against naive RLAIF, and it measures how the policy exploits judge errors. This is a different method (RL from a weak judge, not fine-tuning on weak labels) aimed at the same question. Ground-truth labels are used only for evaluation and the RLVR roofline.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that further weakening the judge speeds hacking, but an extra debate round partly compensates. Add also that the authors frame the setup as a weaker judge overseeing a stronger policy that quickly surpasses it.
record.recipe_differences: Uses full-parameter RL from frozen LLM-judge rewards, including a shared-policy debate protocol, rather than fine-tuning on weak-model labels. The reported 45% gap-recovered calculation compares Debate-AB with RLAIF-A and the RLVR roofline.
record.method_sensitivity: Judge strength changes outcomes: weakening the judge makes AB less robust, while adding an ABA rebuttal improves MCC stability and can nearly recover standard-judge AB accuracy. Critique word limits and judge response constraints are also varied; the text reports that limits up to 150 words stabilize debate, while removing limits allowed critic verbosity to exploit judge bias.

fits_no_version.finding: RL with an LLM judge shows a smaller train/validation reward gap than RLVR. The gap widens with a 20% training subset.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weak-judge reward generalises across prompts more easily than verifiable maths skill.

fits_no_version.finding: RL incentives override prompted misalignment of the players.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RL with a weak judge recovers accuracy despite a misaligned initial prompt.

record.problems: The study tests proprietary mathematics data and one policy family; the main comparison pools multiple debate settings and reports one RLVR run. The authors note that pooled peak-accuracy posteriors may be overconfident because multiple rollouts per question are correlated. It is unclear whether results transfer to non-verifiable or subjective domains, and the reported 45% gap calculation is not the original weak-supervisor PGR measure.
record.rows_left_out: No separately extracted row for the RLVR train/validation reward gap, the alternative pairwise-preference and step-by-step baselines, or the ground-truth Bob experiments: these do not directly test the weak-supervisor-to-strong-student claim versions. Figure-only curve values were not transcribed where the text supplied qualitative results instead.

untested.parts: Fine-tuning on hard labels produced by a weak model; the original PGR formula is not reported by the paper.
Auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling of weak supervisors, loss variants.
Sweeps of supervisor or student size, tasks other than maths (NLP, chess, reward modelling), representation-based predictors of PGR.
Distribution shift; error correlation between weak and strong models.

missing.what: RLVR roofline peak accuracy of 0.7730 (95% CI lower bound 0.7585), needed as the strong ceiling to compute a PGR-style value
Pairwise-preference and step-by-step formatting methods underperformed RLAIF-A; pairwise hacked faster
Preliminary debate variants (draws, frozen API critic) did no better than RLAIF-A; debate without word limits gave critic verbosity hacking
Standard judge: ABA gave no advantage over AB

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for this claim. The policy starts slightly below the judge and overtakes it only through RL. The paper's 45% gap figure uses RLAIF-A as the baseline; the PGR-style values in this verdict are our own calculations. Statistics pool correlated rollouts, so P(best) is overconfident, as the authors note. Figure-only curves for the weak-judge results are not numerically readable.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune on a dataset of hard labels produced by the weaker model; feedback is an LLM judge's RL reward. The reported 45% gap uses RLAIF-A rather than the weaker judge as the baseline.
No auxiliary confidence loss, weak-supervisor ensembling, or loss-variant comparison is reported.
Tests a weakened-judge condition and additional debate rounds on mathematics, but not student-size sweeps, representation predictors, or other tasks such as NLP, chess, and reward modelling.
Tests judge exploitation and the effect of weakening the judge, but not distribution shift or error-correlation between weak and strong models.
No theoretical conditions for a student to beat its supervisor are derived or tested.
No vision or other non-language modality is tested.

rows.note: The paper also reports 65.64% on the training set. This is the weak judge's own generator accuracy, not a weak-label fine-tuning result.
rows.check: This is the weak supervisor's own generator accuracy (66.70% validation, 65.64% train). It is the V1 baseline, not a result, so it should be the baseline field of r2 and r3 rather than a row.

rows.subject: Gemini 2.5 Flash-class policy, RLAIF-A
rows.operation_detail: Single-player RLAIF training with a frozen Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite judge
rows.baseline: Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite generator validation accuracy: 66.70%
rows.note: Table 1 reports peak accuracy as a proportion. The judge generator accuracy is reported separately in Section 3.6.
rows.check: Link and state are correct. The 0.7263 peak beats the judge's 66.70% generator accuracy. The strong ceiling (RLVR 0.7730, Table 1) is not recorded. With it, a PGR-style value is about (0.726−0.667)/(0.773−0.667) ≈ 0.56; this is our own calculation, not the paper's.

rows.subject: Gemini 2.5 Flash-class policy, Debate-AB
rows.operation_detail: Shared-policy self-play as Alice and Bob, with a frozen Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite judge

conditions.value: 50, 100, and 150 words, plus one custom-prompt run pooled

rows.baseline: RLAIF-A peak accuracy 0.7263; Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite generator validation accuracy 66.70%
rows.note: The authors report Debate-AB's peak as about 2 percentage points above RLAIF-A and roughly 45% of the gap to the RLVR roofline. Their gap calculation uses RLAIF-A, not weak-judge generator accuracy.
rows.check: Peak accuracy does not measure judge exploitation, so V4 should be removed. The row bears on V2: debate is a training change that beats naive RLAIF-A (0.7474 vs 0.7263, P(best) 0.9987, 45% of the RLAIF-A-to-RLVR gap). Against the weak judge, the PGR-style value is about 0.76 (our calculation). The pooled debate group mixes word limits of 50, 100 and 150 plus a custom-prompt run.

relation.reason: Reports policy accuracy relative to the weaker judge, training-protocol comparisons, judge-weakness interventions and measured reward hacking.

tranche.reason: Tests stronger-policy learning under weaker-model supervision and exploitation using RL judge rewards and debate, a different method aimed at the same oversight question.

source_check.notes: Evidence concerns RL from weak-judge rewards, rather than the original weak-label fine-tuning recipe; the reported 45% gap recovery is relative to RLAIF-A. Appendix A.3 warns that correlated within-question rollouts inflate effective sample size and make P(Best) overconfident.

statements.correction: Table 1: Debate-AB peak validation accuracy 0.7474; RLAIF-A 0.7263; RLVR 0.7730. Approximately 45% recovery of the RLAIF-A-to-RLVR gap. Weakened-judge ordering ABA > AB > A for MCC stability, transferring to validation accuracy. No weak-label SFT comparator.
statements.problem: The study supports an interactive RL training improvement, but its comparator is RLAIF-A; it does not compare debate training against one-shot weak-label SFT.

statements.correction: Section 4.4: debate permitting draws or using frozen API critics performs similarly to or worse than RLAIF-A. Introduction and Section 5.2: unconstrained critiques exploit judge verbosity bias. No comparison of debate-generated training labels against ordinary weak labels.
statements.problem: The reported negative results are accurate, but this study tests RL training protocols rather than constructing labels for subsequent weak-label fine-tuning.

statements.correction: RLAIF-A baseline; Debate-AB intervention; RLVR roofline; additional standard-versus-weakened-judge comparisons. Baseline impersonation approximately 90% at 30% of training and almost 100% at 60%.
statements.problem: The exploitation results are correct, but the unqualified statement that this study has no controls overlooks its baseline and roofline comparison conditions.
